title: New Year, Hogmanay and Twelfth Night
when_text: 31 December to Twelfth Night (5 January) and Epiphany (6 January); the Old New Year is kept on 11-13 January, and Up Helly Aa on the last Tuesday of January
intro: The turn of the year is kept with fire, football and visiting. Scotland, where the church long frowned on Christmas, made Hogmanay its great winter holiday, and several towns there and in Wales still keep the New Year of the old Julian calendar in mid-January. In England the season ends at Twelfth Night with wassailing in the orchards and rough street games.

facts.title: Where the word Hogmanay comes from
facts.text: Nobody is sure where 'Hogmanay' comes from: French, Norse and Gaelic roots have all been proposed. It is first written down in Yorkshire in 1443, and in Scots in the records of Elgin in 1604. A Manx New Year song with the refrain 'Hogunnaa' has also been recorded.

sources.title: Hogmanay (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The word is first recorded in a Latin entry in 1443 in the West Riding of Yorkshire as hagnonayse. The first appearance in Scots language came in 1604 in the records of Elgin, as hagmonay.

sources.title: Hogmanay (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Frazer and Kelley report a Manx new-year song that begins with the line To-night is New Year's Night, Hogunnaa

facts.title: First-footing
facts.text: Just after midnight people go to be the first across a friend's or neighbour's threshold in the new year, bringing gifts such as coal, shortbread, whisky or black bun. The first-foot is thought to set the household's luck for the year, and a tall, dark-haired man is the luckiest.

sources.title: Hogmanay (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: This involves being the first person to cross the threshold of a friend or neighbour and often involves the giving of symbolic gifts such as salt (less common today), coal, shortbread, whisky, and black bun

sources.title: Hogmanay (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Traditionally, tall, dark-haired men are preferred as the first-foot.

facts.title: An old song taken down from an old man
facts.text: 'Auld Lang Syne', sung at midnight with arms crossed, is a poem Robert Burns wrote in 1788 on an older folk song. He told the Scots Musical Museum he had taken it down from an old man, though some of the words are his own.

sources.title: Auld Lang Syne (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The text is a Scots-language poem written by Robert Burns in 1788, but it is based on an older Scottish folk song.

sources.title: Auld Lang Syne (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: which has never been in print, nor even in manuscript until I took it down from an old man.

facts.title: Swinging fireballs in Stonehaven
facts.text: In Stonehaven, Aberdeenshire, people make balls of chicken wire stuffed with paper, sticks and rags on a length of wire or chain. When the Old Town House bell rings in the new year they light them and swing them round their heads up the High Street from the Mercat Cross and back.

sources.title: Hogmanay (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: As the Old Town House bell sounds to mark the new year, the balls are set alight, and the swingers set off up the High Street from the Mercat Cross to the Cannon and back, swinging the burning balls around their heads as they go.

facts.title: The Burning of the Clavie on the old New Year's Eve
facts.text: When Britain moved to the Gregorian calendar in 1752 the old New Year's Day fell on 12 January, and Burghead in Moray still burns the Clavie, a blazing barrel, on 11 January, the old New Year's Eve. It ends on Doorie Hill, part of the ramparts of the Pictish fort, where embers are handed out for luck. The custom is thought to go back to at least the seventeenth century.

sources.title: Burghead (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Burning of the Clavie continues to be celebrated on "old" New Year's Eve—that is, in the new calendar, on 11 January.

sources.title: Burghead (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: it is thought that the festival dates back to the 17th century, although it could easily predate this by several centuries

facts.title: Tar barrels in Allendale
facts.text: At Allendale in Northumberland the New Year is seen in by guisers carrying burning tar barrels on their heads. The custom is thought to be old, but it can only be traced for certain to the mid-nineteenth century.

sources.title: Allendale Town (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The town's New Year celebrations involve lighted tar barrels that are carried on the heads of revellers called guisers.

sources.title: Allendale Town (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: with definitive evidence only back to the mid-1800s

facts.title: The Ba' in Kirkwall
facts.text: On Christmas Day and New Year's Day Kirkwall plays the Ba', a mass football game between the Uppies and the Doonies through the town streets. The ball is thrown up at the Mercat Cross in front of St Magnus Cathedral.

sources.title: Kirkwall Ba' game (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The games are played twice a year, normally on Christmas Day and New Year's Day

facts.title: Calennig: New Year gifts in Wales
facts.text: In Wales children went from house to house on New Year's Day with an apple stuck with nuts and set on three sticks, singing a verse in return for money or food. The Welsh word calennig, a New Year gift, comes from the Latin kalends, like the English 'calendar'.

sources.title: Calennig (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is a tradition where children carry a decorated apple, pierced with three sticks and decorated with a sprig of box and hazelnuts on New Year's Day.

facts.title: Hen Galan in the Gwaun valley
facts.text: In Cwm Gwaun in Pembrokeshire people still keep New Year by the calendar used before 1752, on 13 January. Children sing Welsh songs from house to house and are given sweets and money, their calennig.

sources.title: Cwm Gwaun (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The locals continue to follow the tradition of the pre-1752 Julian calendar and celebrate New Year (Welsh: Hen Galan) on 13 January.

facts.title: The Mari Lwyd
facts.text: In south Wales a horse's skull on a pole, its bearer hidden under a white sheet, was taken round the houses at Christmas and New Year. The party had to win entry in a battle of sung verses, the pwnco. The custom is first recorded in 1800, faded in the twentieth century and has since been revived.

sources.title: Mari Lwyd (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The custom was first recorded in 1800, with subsequent accounts of it being produced into the early twentieth century.

sources.title: Mari Lwyd (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: it was revived in new forms in the mid-to-latter part of the century

facts.title: Wassailing the apple trees
facts.text: In the cider counties of England, and in Jersey, people sing and drink to the health of the apple trees on Twelfth Night so that they bear well. 'Wassail' itself, from the greeting 'be well', is first recorded around 1140.

sources.title: Wassailing (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Wassailing is also a traditional event in Jersey, Channel Islands where cider (cidre) made up the bulk of the economy before the 20th century.

sources.title: Wassailing (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest record is of around 1140, in Geoffrey of Monmouth's telling of the Rowena story

facts.title: Twelfth cake
facts.text: A bean and a pea were baked into the Twelfth Night cake: whoever found the bean was king for the night, and whoever found the pea, queen. At the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, the actor Robert Baddeley's bequest has paid for cake and punch for the company on 6 January since 1795.

sources.title: Twelfth Night (holiday) (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A popular Twelfth Night tradition was to have a bean and pea hidden inside a Twelfth-night cake

sources.title: Twelfth Night (holiday) (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Theatre Royal, Drury Lane in London has had a tradition since 1795 of providing a cake for the company on Twelfth Night.

facts.title: The Haxey Hood
facts.text: On 6 January a huge scrum, the sway, pushes a leather tube, the hood, to one of the pubs of Haxey in Lincolnshire. The story told is that in the fourteenth century Lady de Mowbray's silk hood blew off and thirteen farm workers chased it; the game's Fool still makes his speech standing on the Mowbray Stone by the church, while damp straw is set smoking behind him.

sources.title: Haxey Hood (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The game is played on 6 January, the Twelfth Day of Christmas

sources.title: Haxey Hood (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: As she went over the hill her silk riding hood was blown away by the wind. Thirteen farm workers in the field rushed to help and chased the hood all over the field.

facts.title: Up Helly Aa is Victorian
facts.text: Lerwick's Up Helly Aa, on the last Tuesday of January, ends the Yule season by burning a Viking galley. The Viking theme is Victorian: the torch processions replaced tar-barrelling from the late 1870s and the first galley was burned in 1889.

sources.title: Up Helly Aa (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first galley was fabricated and burned in 1889.

sources.title: Up Helly Aa (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: who march through the streets of Lerwick on the last Tuesday in January

places.name: Tron Kirk
places.why: The church on Edinburgh's Royal Mile whose spire clock made it the traditional gathering place to see in the New Year.

sources.title: Tron Kirk (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Traditionally the Tron was a place of gathering to celebrate New Year, mainly because of its chiming clock

places.name: Market Cross, High Street, Stonehaven

sources.title: Hogmanay (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the swingers set off up the High Street from the Mercat Cross to the Cannon and back

places.name: Burghead Fort
places.why: The Clavie ends its round on Doorie Hill, the last piece of the fort's southern rampart.

sources.title: Burghead (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: At the end of the route the Clavie is put onto a stone altar (which was not constructed until the 19th century) upon Doorie Hill

sources.title: Burghead (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Doorie Hill (see below), which marked the junction of the citadel and the bailey, is the only remaining piece of the southern ramparts.

places.name: St Magnus Cathedral, Kirkwall
places.why: The Ba' is thrown up at the Mercat Cross on the Kirk Green in front of the cathedral.

sources.title: Kirkwall Ba' game (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Boys Ba' is thrown up from the Merket Cross on the Kirk Green on front of St Magnus Cathedral

places.name: Lerwick Town Hall
places.why: Prince Alfred laid its foundation stone on 24 January 1882, and that evening Lerwick held an Up Helly Aa torchlight procession, by one account the first.

sources.title: Lerwick Town Hall (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: That same evening Lerwick saw the first ever Up Helly Aa torchlight procession.

places.name: Church of St Nicholas, Haxey
places.why: Haxey's Grade I parish church, before which the Fool of the Haxey Hood makes his speech on the Mowbray Stone.

sources.title: Haxey Hood (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the Fool makes his traditional speech of welcome standing on an old mounting block in front of the church known as the Mowbray Stone

sources.title: Haxey (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The town's Grade I listed Anglican parish church, dedicated to Saint Nicholas, originates from the 12th and 13th centuries.

places.name: Theatre Royal, Drury Lane
places.why: The company still cuts the Baddeley Cake here on Twelfth Night, paid for by the will of the actor Robert Baddeley.

sources.title: Twelfth Night (holiday) (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The will of actor Robert Baddeley made a bequest of £100 to be invested in order to provide cake and punch for the company in residence at the theatre on 6 January for every year in perpetuity.

places.name: Cwm Gwaun
places.why: Pembrokeshire valley that still keeps Hen Galan, the Old New Year, on 13 January.

sources.title: Cwm Gwaun (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Children walk from house to house, and sing traditional Welsh language songs.
